name: Melanesian
era: From about 50,000 years ago to today
line: Tend your garden, arrive with a gift, answer your wantok and pass on what you are given.

quote.text: Our identity lies ahead of us.
quote.source: The Kanak leader of New Caledonia, in an interview of 1985. He meant that a people’s culture is something they go on making

quotes.text: We, the people of Papua New Guinea, united in one nation, pay homage to the memory of our ancestors, the source of our strength and origin of our combined heritage.
quotes.by: The Constitution of Papua New Guinea

quotes.text: Once in the Kula, always in the Kula.
quotes.source: As reported from the Trobriand Islands by Bronisław Malinowski, Argonauts of the Western Pacific, 1922

quotes.by: National motto of Papua New Guinea
quotes.source: A country of more than eight hundred languages

quotes.text: To grasp the native’s point of view, his relation to life, to realise his vision of his world.
quotes.source: His statement of the aim of fieldwork, Argonauts of the Western Pacific, 1922. An outsider’s words, and of their time

words.meaning: One talk; someone of your own language
words.usage: A person from your language group, village or region, and so someone you must help and may call on. The wantok system is the social security of Melanesia.

words.meaning: Custom; the ways of the ancestors
words.usage: Traditional law, ceremony, knowledge and land rights taken together. People speak of following kastom as against the ways of the state or the church.
You and me. The form of we that includes the person spoken to. The national anthem of Vanuatu begins with it three times.
Talk of the place. One’s mother tongue, as against the shared pidgin or English.
The place where a person’s land, kin and ancestors are, however long they have lived in town.
A man who leads because of what he has achieved and given away, not by birth. He must go on persuading and providing to keep his name.
Made by women from plant fibre or wool and carried from the forehead. It holds babies, garden food and everything else. The word also means womb.

words.meaning: A gathering for dance and song
words.usage: Groups in paint, feathers and shells perform their own dances. Held for exchanges, peacemakings and now for shows.

words.meaning: An earth oven; a feast cooked in one
words.usage: Pork, sweet potato and greens steamed in a pit on hot stones under banana leaves.
To offer kaikai is the first act of welcome.
Unhurried conversation. Sitting down to stori is how news travels and how relationships are kept up.
A place or thing that is set apart, and a relative by marriage, who must be treated with reserve. Among the Tolai it is also the name of shell money.
The tall, painted ceremonial house of villages along the Sepik river, where the men’s ritual objects are kept.
A settled, peaceful life with enough food, good relations and no trouble.
Among the islands off eastern New Guinea, red shell necklaces travel clockwise and white armshells the other way, from partner to partner, for ever.

words.meaning: A gift that must be bettered
words.usage: In the highlands around Mount Hagen, pigs and shells are given in public, and the receiver must later give back more.

words.meaning: The land, its people and their custom
words.usage: One word for all three. A Fijian belongs to a vanua and cannot be understood apart from it.
The Fijian greeting. Ni sa bula is the full form.
Vinaka vaka levu is thank you very much.
The root of a pepper plant, pounded and mixed with water in a wooden bowl and drunk at every meeting.

words.meaning: The presenting of kava by a guest
words.usage: A visitor offers a bundle of root to the chief of a village and asks leave to enter. Once it is accepted, the visitor is under the village’s care.

words.meaning: A request that should not be refused
words.usage: Asking a relative for something you need. The giver may ask in turn another day.

words.meaning: Working together for the common good
words.usage: The whole village turns out to build a house, plant a garden or prepare a feast, with no payment.
The most valued object in Fiji, presented at marriages, deaths and apologies. It may not be taken out of the country without a permit.
The men’s house or shaded ground where a village in Vanuatu settles its affairs and drinks kava at dusk.
The cleared ceremonial ground of a village, often beside a great banyan tree.
A hollowed log with a carved face, set upright in the ground on Ambrym and nearby islands and beaten to call people together.

words.meaning: A baked pudding of grated root
words.usage: Yam, taro or banana grated, soaked in coconut cream and baked in leaves. The national dish of Vanuatu.
Tru means truly.
The usual goodbye.

practices.name: Tend your garden
practices.instructions: Spend half an hour this morning growing food. Dig, plant, weed, water or harvest, in a garden, an allotment, or a few pots on a sill if that is all you have. Work with your hands in the soil. Notice which plants are doing well and which need help. The rule of this Onda is to grow some of your own food.
practices.why: Gardens are central to Melanesian life, from the yam and taro gardens of the islands to the sweet potato fields of the New Guinea highlands, where farming began 7,000 years ago.
variations: Plant a bean in a pot.
Share a vegetable with a neighbour.

practices.name: Arrive with a gift
practices.instructions: Wherever you go today as a visitor, to a home, an office or a meeting, do not arrive with empty hands. Bring something small to share: food, fruit, something you made. On arriving, greet the person whose place it is before anyone else. The rule of this Onda is never to arrive empty-handed.
practices.why: Across Melanesia a visitor brings a gift, a pig, a mat, a bundle of food, and the host gives something back. Gifts build the relationship.

practices.name: A message to your wantok
practices.instructions: Write or call a wantok today: a relative, a friend, a person from your village, school or street who is one of your own people. In Tok Pisin wantok means one talk, someone who speaks your language and to whom you owe help and from whom you can ask. Ask how they are, and ask if they need something. The rule of this Onda is to answer your wantok.
practices.why: The wantok system is the web of obligations and kinship that holds Melanesian societies together. It can also be a burden, but at its best it is mutual care.
variations: Ask for help with something small.

practices.name: Kaikai: sweet potato breakfast
practices.instructions: Eat a breakfast of kaikai, food, in the Melanesian way: bake or boil a sweet potato, a taro or a banana, and eat it with a little coconut cream or salt. Peel it with your fingers. Eat slowly and give thanks to the garden. Sweet potato is the staple of the New Guinea highlands.
practices.why: The kumul or sweet potato feeds millions in Papua New Guinea. A simple breakfast of root vegetables is a link to the garden.

practices.name: A word of Tok Pisin
practices.instructions: Learn one Tok Pisin word or phrase today: gutpela moning, good morning; tenkyu tru, thank you very much; lukim yu, see you; yumi, we together; wantok; kaikai; stori. Tok Pisin is an English-based creole spoken by millions in Papua New Guinea. Say it aloud to someone.
practices.why: Tok Pisin is the lingua franca of Papua New Guinea, and a lively, easy language for English speakers. A few words go a long way.
variations: Say the phrases to a friend.
Read a headline in Tok Pisin.

practices.name: Stand on your own ground
practices.instructions: Go outside and stand barefoot on the ground for five minutes. Ples, place, is central to Melanesian identity, the land you come from and belong to. Name the place, its trees, hills and water. Think of who has lived there before you. In Fijian the idea is vanua, land, people and customs as one.
practices.why: Land is the basis of identity and belonging across Melanesia, from Papua New Guinea to Fiji. Standing on ground you care about is a quiet way to feel it.
variations: Look up the old name of your place.

practices.name: Work together on one person’s job
practices.instructions: Give half an hour of your labour today to someone else’s task. Help a neighbour to move, dig, paint, cook for a crowd or mind children. Or call on others to help with a job of your own, and feed them afterwards. Work side by side and talk as you go. In Tok Pisin the word is wok bung, working together.
practices.why: Work together on one person’s job is a classic Melanesian form of cooperation. In Fiji the word is solesolevaki, and in Papua New Guinea wok bung.
variations: Help a neighbour with a garden.
Ask friends to help you clear a space.

practices.name: Pass it on
practices.instructions: Give something away today that was given to you. It might be a book, a tool, a present you have enjoyed, money that came unexpectedly or a kindness someone did you. Choose a person, hand it over in person and tell them where it came from. Gifts in Melanesia keep moving: you hold them, you do not hoard them. The rule of this Onda is to give to gain a name.
practices.why: In Melanesian exchange systems, such as the moka of the highlands, gifts circulate, and the givers earn respect and a name. Passing on what you were given keeps it alive.
variations: Tell the story of the gift.

practices.name: Loop a bilum
practices.instructions: Make a small bilum, the looped string bag that women of Papua New Guinea make from plant fibre or wool. Take a ball of string or yarn and make a chain of loops with your fingers, then loop each row into the one before, in a spiral, to form a small bag or pouch. It takes patience. Give it to a friend or use it daily.
practices.why: The bilum is the iconic bag of Papua New Guinea, made by women and carried everywhere, even used for babies. It is also a unique art form.
variations: Learn from a video by a PNG maker.

practices.name: String figures
practices.instructions: Play with string figures: loop a piece of string and make shapes between your fingers, such as the cat’s cradle. In Melanesia string figures tell stories: a bird, a fish, a house. Learn one from a friend or video, and tell a story as you make it. Pass it to another person. Play with children if you can.
practices.why: String figures are made across Melanesia and the Pacific, and each carries a story. They are a lovely way to share a tale with your hands.
variations: Make a figure and tell a tale.

practices.name: Settle it and eat together
practices.instructions: If you have a quarrel, resolve it today by talking it out and sharing food. In Melanesia disputes are settled by community discussion, with compensation if needed, and the resolution is sealed by a shared meal. Choose a conflict, find the other person, listen to their account and agree a repair. Then eat.
practices.why: Settling disputes by talk, compensation and a shared meal is a traditional Melanesian approach, aimed at restoring relationships rather than punishing. It is practical wisdom.
variations: Share a meal at the end.

practices.name: A team game with your own rules
practices.instructions: Invent a simple team game with friends, with rules that everyone agrees, and play it. In the Trobriand Islands people took up cricket and changed the rules: any number of players, dances, war paint and a home team that always wins. Play for fun, make up the rules as you go and laugh. Keep it friendly.
practices.why: Trobriand cricket is a famous example of a game remade to local custom. Making your own version is a way of owning a game.

practices.name: Sit down and stori
practices.instructions: When the day’s work is done, eat with other people and then stay sitting. Share out the food so that everyone has some before anyone has seconds. Then talk with no purpose: what happened today, who was seen, an old story, a joke. In Tok Pisin this is stori. The rule of this Onda is to share food.
practices.why: To stori is to tell stories and talk, a central social act in Melanesia. Sitting around the evening fire or table is the heart of community.
variations: Ask an elder to tell one.

practices.name: Singsing
practices.instructions: Sing together, in the manner of a singsing, a gathering of song and dance. Choose a simple song with a chorus, a hymn, a folk song or a pop song, and sing it as a group, clapping and swaying. The singsing is the heart of Melanesian festivals. Sing out. If you are alone, sing along to a recording.
practices.why: Singsing is the Tok Pisin word for a festival of song and dance, with elaborate costumes. A simple singalong is the home version.

practices.name: Listen to the panpipes
practices.instructions: Play ’Are’are panpipe music from Malaita in the Solomon Islands, or the water music of the women of Vanuatu. Listen with your eyes closed to the interlocking pipes or the splashes of hands on water. These sounds are ancient and unique. Sit still and let them wash over you.
practices.why: The ’Are’are panpipe ensembles are among the most complex music in the Pacific. Vanuatu’s women make music by slapping the water.
variations: Look at a picture of the pipes.
Slap water in a bath for rhythm.

practices.name: Share the food fairly
practices.instructions: At the evening meal, share out the food so that everyone has a portion before anyone has seconds. Serve the guests, children and elders first. Share a little with a neighbour. In Melanesian custom the host’s generosity is a matter of pride. Eat together, and wait for everyone before starting.
practices.why: Sharing food is the basis of social life in Melanesia. A shared meal makes and mends relationships.
variations: Cook a dish for several households.

practices.name: Tell the story of your place
practices.instructions: Tell a story about the place where you live: how it got its name, who lived there, what happened. In Melanesia every place has a story, and the stories belong to the people of that place. Tell yours, or ask an older neighbour to tell theirs. Write it down.
practices.why: Place stories are central to Melanesian identity and belong to specific peoples. Telling the stories of your own place is a respectful way to join in.
variations: Draw a map of the story.

practices.name: Say lukim yu properly
practices.instructions: When someone leaves you today, or when you part at night, say lukim yu, see you, with a gift or a kind word. Never part with a quarrel. Hold their hand for a moment. In Melanesia leave-taking is a social act, with time given to it and promises to meet again. Say the farewell with care.
practices.why: Leave-takings in Melanesia are warm and unhurried. Parting well keeps the relationship intact.
variations: Say when you will meet again.

practices.name: A mumu-style feast
practices.instructions: Cook a feast in the spirit of the mumu, the earth oven of Papua New Guinea. At home use a large covered pot or an oven tray: layer sweet potato, taro, greens, pumpkin and chicken or fish, wrapped in banana leaves or foil, with coconut cream. Invite neighbours and friends, share the cooking and serve everyone before you eat.
practices.why: The mumu is cooked underground with hot stones for feasts and festivals. A shared meal in the spirit of it celebrates community.

practices.name: A day in the garden
practices.instructions: Spend a morning in a garden with friends or family, digging, planting and weeding, then eat what you grow, or buy together. In Melanesia the garden is the centre of life and each family’s plot is a matter of pride. Share the work and the produce, and end with a meal. Plant something to harvest later.
practices.why: Gardening is the daily work of most Melanesians and a delight. A shared day of it brings food and friendship.
variations: Plant yam or taro if you can.

immersePlan.name: Read from The Melanesian Way
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Bernard Narokobi’s 1980 book by a Papua New Guinean lawyer and writer on Melanesian values. Note one idea.

immersePlan.name: Read from Kiki
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Albert Maori Kiki’s 1968 autobiography, the first by a Papua New Guinean. Note how he writes of change.

immersePlan.name: Read from Black Stone
immersePlan.text: Read poems of Grace Mera Molisa of Vanuatu, a bold voice. Read one aloud.

immersePlan.name: Watch Tanna
immersePlan.text: Watch the 2015 film shot on Tanna in Vanuatu with the Yakel people, a love story based on a true event. The volcano glows.

immersePlan.name: Watch Trobriand Cricket
immersePlan.text: Watch the 1975 film of Trobriand Islanders playing their version of cricket, with dancing and magic. It is funny and clever.

immersePlan.name: Watch First Contact
immersePlan.text: Watch the 1983 documentary on the 1930s meeting of Australian gold prospectors and highland peoples, told by those who were there. A serious film.

immersePlan.name: Listen to the ’Are’are panpipes
immersePlan.text: Play the panpipe ensembles of Malaita. Listen to the interlocking sound.

immersePlan.name: Listen to George Telek
immersePlan.text: Play the 1997 album by the Tolai singer from Papua New Guinea, mixing traditional and modern. Sing along.

immersePlan.name: Listen to the water music of Vanuatu
immersePlan.text: Play a recording of the women of Gaua splashing, slapping and drumming the water. Try it in a bowl.

immersePlan.name: Look at malagan carvings
immersePlan.text: Look at the intricate carvings made in northern New Ireland for memorial ceremonies, which are often destroyed after use.

immersePlan.name: Look at bilums
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of looped string bags in brilliant patterns from Papua New Guinea. Pick a pattern to copy.

immersePlan.name: Look at Mathias Kauage’s paintings
immersePlan.text: Look at the vivid, busy paintings of Papua New Guinea’s best-known painter, Kauage, who called himself the Big Man of PNG art. This artist has passed away.

immersePlan.name: Cook a mumu-style meal
immersePlan.text: Cook pork or chicken with sweet potato and greens in a covered pot. Share it.

immersePlan.name: Make laplap
immersePlan.text: Grate yam, banana or cassava, wrap it in leaves with coconut cream and bake. It is the national dish of Vanuatu.

immersePlan.name: Make kokoda
immersePlan.text: Marinate raw fish in lime juice, then add coconut cream, tomato and onion. Eat it cold with taro.

immersePlan.name: Learn about kava
immersePlan.text: Read about kava, drunk from coconut shells in Fiji, Vanuatu and other places. As a guest, drink it only when invited, and avoid it with medication or liver problems.

immersePlan.name: Drink a green coconut
immersePlan.text: Drink from a young green coconut and scrape out the flesh. Share one.

immersePlan.name: Drink a cup of PNG coffee
immersePlan.text: Drink a cup of coffee from Papua New Guinea’s highlands, grown by small farmers around Goroka. Notice the taste.

immersePlan.name: Learn about sevusevu
immersePlan.text: Read about the Fijian custom of presenting kava roots to the chief on arriving in a village. Bring a gift to your next visit.

immersePlan.name: Learn about compensation
immersePlan.text: Read how disputes in Melanesia are ended by payment and a shared meal. Think of a quarrel you could mend with a gift.

immersePlan.name: Learn about shell money
immersePlan.text: Read about the strings of shells used as money in New Ireland and the Solomon Islands. Make a necklace of beads.

immersePlan.name: Play Trobriand cricket
immersePlan.text: Play a game of cricket or rounders with your own rules: any number of players, chants and a home team that wins.

immersePlan.name: Make a string figure
immersePlan.text: Make a cat’s cradle or another figure from a loop of string. Tell a tale as you make it.

immersePlan.name: Play or watch rugby sevens
immersePlan.text: Fiji’s national sport is rugby sevens, played at speed. Watch a clip, or throw a ball with friends.

immersePlan.name: Look up the Goroka Show
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the great highlands cultural show in Papua New Guinea with hundreds of tribal groups in costume.

immersePlan.name: Look up Hiri Moale
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the festival in Port Moresby celebrating the old trading voyages of the Motu in lagatoi canoes.

immersePlan.name: Look up the Tjibaou Cultural Centre
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the museum in Nouméa designed by Renzo Piano to honour Kanak culture. Notice the shell-like huts.

immersePlan.name: Practise wantok
immersePlan.text: Wantok means one talk, a relative or person of your own people. Do something for your wantok today.

immersePlan.name: Practise stori
immersePlan.text: Stori is telling stories and talking. Spend half an hour in easy talk with others.

immersePlan.name: Think about kastom
immersePlan.text: Kastom is tradition and custom. Name one custom you keep, and why.

rules.text: Grow some of your own food
rules.why: Put your hands in the soil. A person with a garden is never poor.
Bring a gift and ask leave. Every place has its owners.
When your own people ask, help. You will ask in your turn.
Standing comes from what you give away, not from what you keep.
Do not eat alone while others are present.
Make good a wrong with a gift, and seal the peace with a meal.

read.title: The Melanesian Way
read.creator: Bernard Narokobi
read.why: Newspaper essays by a lawyer and philosopher from the Sepik, arguing that Melanesians have their own vision of life and should build a nation on it.

read.title: Kiki: Ten Thousand Years in a Lifetime
read.creator: Albert Maori Kiki
read.why: A man born into a society without metal becomes a medical worker, trade unionist and minister of state. He tells it plainly.

read.title: The Crocodile
read.creator: Vincent Eri
read.why: The first novel by a Papua New Guinean. A young man from the Gulf is taken as a carrier in the war.

read.title: Black Stone
read.creator: Grace Mera Molisa
read.why: Sharp, spare poems on colonialism, independence and the place of women, by Vanuatu’s foremost poet.

read.title: Kanaky
read.creator: Jean-Marie Tjibaou
read.why: Speeches, interviews and writings of the Kanak leader on culture, land and independence.

read.title: Argonauts of the Western Pacific
read.creator: Bronisław Malinowski
read.why: The classic description of the Kula, by an anthropologist who lived for two years in the Trobriand Islands.

watch.title: First Contact
watch.creator: Bob Connolly and Robin Anderson
watch.why: Film shot by Australian gold prospectors entering the New Guinea highlands in the 1930s, shown fifty years later to the people who appear in it.

watch.title: Tanna
watch.creator: Bentley Dean and Martin Butler, with the people of Yakel
watch.why: A true story of two lovers who defied an arranged marriage, acted by the villagers in their own language on their own island.

watch.title: Trobriand Cricket: An Ingenious Response to Colonialism
watch.creator: Gary Kildea and Jerry Leach
watch.why: How islanders took a missionary game and made it a ritual of dance, magic and exchange.

watch.title: Ophir
watch.creator: Alexandre Berman and Olivier Pollet
watch.why: The people of Bougainville tell the story of the mine, the war and their struggle for independence.

listen.title: Solomon Islands: ’Are’are Panpipe Ensembles
listen.creator: Musicians of Malaita, recorded by Hugo Zemp
listen.why: Groups of bamboo pipes of different sizes play interlocking parts, in a music with its own detailed theory.

listen.title: Telek
listen.creator: George Telek
listen.why: Songs in Kuanua and Tok Pisin by a Tolai singer from Rabaul, mixing string band, choir and ritual chant.

listen.title: Water music of Vanuatu
listen.creator: The women of Gaua and Mere Lava
listen.why: Standing waist-deep in the sea, women slap, scoop and plunge their hands to make rhythm and melody from the water.

listen.title: The Blessed Islands: Chants from the Thin Red Line
listen.creator: Choirs of the Melanesian Brotherhood and All Saints, Honiara
listen.why: Hymns in Solomon Islands languages sung in rich, open harmony.

art.title: Malagan carvings
art.creator: Carvers of northern New Ireland
art.why: Intricate openwork figures of birds, fish and ancestors, made for ceremonies that complete the mourning of the dead, displayed briefly and then left to rot or given away.

art.title: The bilum
art.creator: Women throughout Papua New Guinea
art.why: Each region has its own looping patterns and colours. A bilum is given at births, marriages and partings.

art.title: The spirit house front
art.creator: Abelam and Sepik painters
art.why: A triangular façade up to twenty-five metres high, painted with rows of ancestral faces in red, yellow, black and white.

art.title: Paintings of Mathias Kauage
art.creator: Mathias Kauage
art.why: Bright, crowded pictures of helicopters, buses and independence day by a Chimbu man who had been a labourer. The first Papua New Guinean painter known abroad.

eat.title: Mumu
eat.creator: Pork, sweet potato and greens from the earth oven
eat.why: The feast food of the highlands, shared out by name to every group present.

eat.title: Laplap
eat.creator: Grated yam or banana baked with coconut cream
eat.why: Wrapped in leaves and cooked on hot stones. Eaten in slabs with meat or fish on top.

eat.title: Kokoda
eat.creator: Raw fish in lime and coconut cream
eat.why: The Fijian dish, served in a half coconut shell.

eat.title: Sago
eat.creator: Starch washed from the pith of a palm
eat.why: The staple of the swamps and great rivers of New Guinea, made into pancakes or a thick jelly.

drink.title: Kava
drink.creator: Fresh root, ground and mixed with water
drink.why: In Vanuatu it is made from the green root and is strong. It is drunk in one go at dusk, in a quiet nakamal.

drink.title: Green coconut
drink.creator: Kulau
drink.why: Opened with a bush knife and handed to a guest on arrival.

drink.title: Highlands coffee
drink.creator: Arabica from Goroka and Mount Hagen
drink.why: Grown in village gardens since the 1950s and the main cash crop of the highlands.

customs.title: Sevusevu
customs.creator: Kava for the chief
customs.why: A visitor to a Fijian village sits cross-legged while a spokesman presents the root. When it is accepted, hands are clapped with cupped palms.

customs.title: Making la coutume
customs.creator: The Kanak custom gesture
customs.why: On arriving at a tribe in New Caledonia, the guest lays down cloth and a small offering and says a few words. The host answers and the visit can begin.

customs.title: Compensation
customs.creator: Payment to end a wrong
customs.why: An injury or death is settled between groups by a negotiated gift of pigs, shell money or cash, followed by a shared meal.

customs.title: Shell money
customs.creator: Still in use
customs.why: The Tolai of New Britain keep coils of small shells threaded on cane, which pay for brides, funerals and, in some places, school fees.

games.title: Trobriand cricket
games.creator: Team game · Trobriand Islands
games.why: Any number may play, the home side always wins, and each team enters and leaves with a chant and dance of its own.

games.title: String figures
games.creator: Hand game · all Melanesia
games.why: Patterns made in a loop of string, each with a name and often a song. Hundreds have been recorded in Papua New Guinea alone.

games.title: Veitiqa
games.creator: Throwing game · Fiji
games.why: A reed dart with a heavy wooden head is skimmed along a grass track as far as it will go. Villages competed against each other.

games.title: Rugby sevens
games.creator: Ball game · Fiji
games.why: Fiji’s national passion. Its men won the country’s first Olympic medal, a gold, in 2016.

festivals.title: Goroka Show
festivals.creator: The weekend nearest 16 September, Eastern Highlands
festivals.why: More than a hundred groups gather in full dress to dance. It began in 1957 and falls at Independence Day.

festivals.title: Land diving
festivals.creator: Saturdays from April to June, Pentecost Island, Vanuatu
festivals.why: Men leap from a wooden tower up to thirty metres high with vines tied to their ankles, to bless the yam harvest. It belongs to the villages of the south of the island.

festivals.title: Hiri Moale
festivals.creator: September, Port Moresby
festivals.why: The Motu people remember the great trading voyages of their ancestors, who sailed pots west and brought back sago.

festivals.title: Melanesian Arts and Culture Festival
festivals.creator: Every four years
festivals.why: Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, Fiji and New Caledonia take turns to host dancers, carvers and musicians from the whole region.

places.title: Kuk Early Agricultural Site
places.creator: Western Highlands, Papua New Guinea
places.why: Drainage ditches and planting mounds in a swamp, showing farming here for seven to ten thousand years. A World Heritage site.

places.title: Chief Roi Mata’s Domain
places.creator: Efate and nearby islands, Vanuatu
places.why: The home, the place of death and the island grave of a great chief of about 1600, kept under prohibition by his people for four centuries.

places.title: Tjibaou Cultural Centre
places.creator: Nouméa, New Caledonia
places.why: Ten tall curved pavilions of wood and steel by Renzo Piano, modelled on the Kanak great house, in a garden that tells the Kanak story of creation.

places.title: The Sepik River
places.creator: Northern Papua New Guinea
places.why: More than a thousand kilometres of river lined with villages of carvers, each with its spirit house.

places.title: Levuka
places.creator: Ovalau, Fiji
places.why: The first colonial capital, a wooden port town beneath steep green hills, and a World Heritage site.

places.title: Mount Yasur
places.creator: Tanna, Vanuatu
places.why: An active volcano whose glow can be seen from the sea. For the people of Tanna it is the house of the spirits.

ethics.title: Reciprocity
ethics.text: Every gift makes a tie, and every tie must be honoured.
ethics.practice: Return something today that you have owed for a while.

ethics.title: Generosity
ethics.text: A great person is one who gives.

ethics.title: Loyalty to kin
ethics.text: Stand by your own people when they need you.
ethics.practice: Call a relative you have neglected.

ethics.title: Respect for land
ethics.text: Land is held from the ancestors for those to come and cannot be sold away.
ethics.practice: Learn who the first owners of your land were.

ethics.title: Cooperation
ethics.text: Big work is done by everyone together.
ethics.practice: Join in something you would rather leave to others.

ethics.title: Peacemaking
ethics.text: A quarrel is ended by making good the loss, in public.
ethics.practice: Offer something concrete to mend a wrong.

philosophy.title: The person as relations
philosophy.text: In Melanesia a person is made up of ties to kin, land and ancestors. Without them one is nobody.
philosophy.practice: Who would you be without your relations?

philosophy.title: Wealth is for giving
philosophy.text: Things gain value by moving. The one who gives most stands highest.
philosophy.practice: What are you holding that should be moving?

philosophy.title: Leadership by achievement
philosophy.text: A big man has no office. He leads only as long as others choose to follow.
philosophy.practice: Whom do you follow freely, and why?

philosophy.title: Land is life
philosophy.text: Nearly all land is still held by clans under custom. It is identity, food and security at once.
philosophy.practice: What could never be bought from you?

philosophy.title: The Melanesian Way
philosophy.text: Narokobi held that Melanesians should not copy the West or the East but draw on their own total view of life.
philosophy.practice: What in your own tradition are you overlooking?

philosophy.title: Many peoples, one house
philosophy.text: More than a thousand languages live side by side. Unity has to be made without sameness.
philosophy.practice: How do you live with people who are not like you?

philosophy.title: Custom moves
philosophy.text: Kastom is not a museum. People choose what to carry forward.
philosophy.practice: Which custom of yours should change?

philosophy.title: The gift and the debt
philosophy.text: The wantok system feeds everyone and can also weigh on those who earn. Obligation cuts both ways.
philosophy.practice: Where does helping your own become unfair to others?

journal: Who are your wantoks, and what do you owe each other?
What did you grow or tend today?

Whose work did you join, and who joined yours?

intro: Melanesia is the arc of islands that runs from New Guinea, the second largest island in the world, eastward through the Bismarck Archipelago and the Solomon Islands to Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji. The name was coined by a French explorer in 1832 from Greek words for black islands, with reference to the skin of the people, and it lumps together peoples who had no common name for themselves. Many have since taken it up with pride. The region is now made up of four independent states, Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu and Fiji, the French territory of New Caledonia, and the western half of New Guinea, which is ruled by Indonesia.

It is among the oldest inhabited places outside Africa. People crossed from Asia to New Guinea about fifty thousand years ago, when it was joined to Australia, and were living in its high valleys soon afterwards. They reached the Solomon Islands some thirty thousand years ago. In the highlands they became some of the world’s first farmers, draining swamps to grow taro, banana and sugar cane at least seven thousand years ago. About 1500 BC a new seafaring people with fine decorated pottery, known as Lapita, appeared in the islands off New Guinea, mixed with those already there and sailed on to settle Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji.

Long separation in mountain valleys and on scattered islands produced a diversity found nowhere else. Papua New Guinea alone has more than eight hundred languages, and the region as a whole perhaps thirteen hundred, a fifth of all the languages on Earth. Shared pidgins grew up to bridge them: Tok Pisin, Bislama and Solomons Pijin.

For all the differences, certain things are common. Most people live in villages and feed themselves from gardens. Land belongs to clans under customary law and is the basis of identity. Society is held together by exchange. Pigs, yams, shell valuables and food are given in public at marriages, funerals and peacemakings, and every gift creates an obligation. In much of the region leaders are not born to office. A big man gains influence by organising, speaking well and giving generously, and loses it when he stops. Fiji and parts of the islands have hereditary chiefs. Ancestors remain present, and striking arts of carving, painting, mask and dance are made for them.

Europeans traded and missionised from the early nineteenth century, and colonial rule by Britain, Germany, France, the Netherlands and Australia followed. Tens of thousands of islanders were taken, often by trickery or force, to work on the sugar plantations of Queensland and Fiji. The highlands of New Guinea, home to a million people, were unknown to the outside world until the 1930s. The Second World War was fought across the region. Independence came between 1970 and 1980. Nearly everyone is now Christian, and church and custom live side by side.
The people of a language group call each other wantok, one talk, and the tie of mutual help it names reaches from the village into the towns.
This Onda takes its practices from everyday life: the garden, the gift on arrival, shared work, passing things on and sitting to talk.

guide.era: People reached New Guinea about 50,000 years ago. Some thirteen million Melanesians live in the region today

figures.name: Roi Mata
figures.bio: A paramount chief of central Vanuatu remembered for ending wars between the clans. His grave, found in 1967 where oral tradition said it would be, held some fifty people buried with him.

figures.name: Ratu Seru Cakobau
figures.bio: The Fijian chief of Bau who became a Christian, claimed kingship over all Fiji and ceded the islands to Britain in 1874.

figures.name: Ratu Sir Lala Sukuna
figures.bio: Fijian chief, soldier and scholar who secured Fijian ownership of land and prepared the way to self-government.

figures.name: Sir Jacob Vouza
figures.bio: A retired police sergeant of Guadalcanal who, captured and bayoneted in 1942, chewed through his ropes and crawled back to warn of an attack.

figures.name: Albert Maori Kiki
figures.bio: From the Gulf of Papua. Pathologist’s assistant, union founder and one of the makers of independence.

figures.name: Sir Michael Somare
figures.bio: A teacher and broadcaster from the Sepik who led Papua New Guinea to independence in 1975 and was four times its prime minister. Known as the Grand Chief.

figures.name: Jean-Marie Tjibaou
figures.bio: A former priest who led the Kanak independence movement, signed a peace accord in 1988 and was assassinated the following year.

figures.name: Dame Josephine Abaijah
figures.bio: The first woman elected to the parliament of Papua New Guinea, in 1972.

figures.name: Walter Lini
figures.bio: An Anglican priest who became the first prime minister of Vanuatu in 1980 and spoke of a Melanesian socialism based on sharing.

figures.name: Bernard Narokobi
figures.bio: Lawyer, philosopher and politician who helped write the constitution of Papua New Guinea and gave the Melanesian Way its name.

figures.name: Mathias Kauage
figures.bio: A painter from Chimbu who recorded the arrival of the modern world in the highlands.

figures.name: Grace Mera Molisa
figures.bio: Poet, politician and campaigner for women, and a signatory of Vanuatu’s constitution.

history.detail: People cross from Asia to the continent of Sahul, which joined New Guinea and Australia. Camps in the highlands are nearly as old.
People reach New Britain, New Ireland and Buka in the northern Solomons, crossing open sea.
Highlanders dig drains and mounds to grow taro and bananas. New Guinea is one of the independent birthplaces of agriculture.
Seafarers with decorated pottery spread from the Bismarck Archipelago to Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji, and on into Polynesia.
Portuguese and Spanish ships touch New Guinea, the Solomons and Vanuatu. Cook charts and names the New Hebrides and New Caledonia.
Jules Dumont d’Urville divides the Pacific into Polynesia, Micronesia and Melanesia.
France annexes the island and makes it a penal colony. Kanak lands are taken, and a great revolt in 1878 is crushed.
Some sixty-two thousand men and women from Vanuatu and the Solomons are taken to cut cane in Queensland. Many are kidnapped or deceived.
Britain takes Fiji and brings Indian labourers to its plantations. New Guinea is divided between the Netherlands, Germany and Britain. Vanuatu is ruled jointly by Britain and France.
Australian prospectors walk into valleys holding a million people whose existence had not been suspected.
Japanese and Allied forces fight along the Kokoda track, on Guadalcanal and across the islands. Islanders serve as carriers, scouts and coastwatchers.
After the Dutch leave, Indonesia confirms its rule through a vote by 1,025 selected delegates. Resistance continues.
Fiji in 1970, Papua New Guinea in 1975, Solomon Islands in 1978 and Vanuatu in 1980.
A war over a copper mine on Bougainville ends in 1998, and in 2019 its people vote overwhelmingly for independence. New Caledonia holds three referendums from 2018.

concepts.detail: Wantoks house, feed and find work for each other and share what they earn. It is a safety net with no state behind it, and a pressure on anyone with a wage or an office.

concepts.text: Giving as the centre of public life.
concepts.detail: The Kula, the moka of the highlands and many other systems move valuables, pigs and food between groups. They make peace, alliances and reputations.
A leader builds a following by helping others meet their obligations and then calls on their support. He commands no one.
The body of law and practice that governs land, marriage and dispute. The constitutions of the independent states recognise it.
In Papua New Guinea about ninety-seven per cent of land is held by clans under custom and cannot be sold outright.
The Fijian idea that a community, its territory, its chiefs and its ways form a single whole.
A wrong is made good by a public gift to the injured group. The aim is to mend the relationship, not to punish.
Ancestors watch over their descendants and the land, and spirits live in particular pools, rocks and trees.
Narokobi’s argument, taken up across the region, that Melanesian values of community, consensus and sharing are a sound basis for a modern nation.

facts.text: Papua New Guinea has about 840 living languages, more than any other country.
Vanuatu has more languages for the size of its population than anywhere on Earth: well over a hundred for some three hundred thousand people.
Sugar cane and the banana were both first cultivated in New Guinea.
The sport of bungee jumping was inspired by the land divers of Pentecost Island.
In 1943 two Solomon Islanders, Biuku Gasa and Eroni Kumana, found the shipwrecked crew of John F. Kennedy’s patrol boat and carried his message, scratched on a coconut, to safety.
The word Kanak comes from kanaka, the Hawaiian word for a person, and was once an insult. The people of New Caledonia took it as their own name in the 1970s.

sensitivity.note: Melanesia holds more than a thousand distinct peoples, and no summary can speak for them. This Onda was written by outsiders from published sources, draws on everyday values held widely across the region, and should be reviewed by Melanesian readers.
requiredCaveats: Every word here comes from a particular language, which is named. Customs of the highlands, the coasts, Vanuatu, the Kanak country and Fiji differ greatly.
Initiations, spirit houses, masks and much ritual knowledge are restricted, often to initiated men or to women. Nothing here asks you to imitate them.
The name Melanesia was given by Europeans on the basis of skin colour. Many people now use it proudly, and many prefer the name of their own people.
Much classic writing on the region is by foreign anthropologists. Read Melanesian authors alongside them. The future of West Papua, Bougainville and New Caledonia is contested and unresolved.
